ideal_client_profile.context: Academic — the audience is an examiner evaluating undergraduate philosophy essays, not a commercial customer

demographics.role: Examiner in an undergraduate Analytic Philosophy programme

primary_values: Conceptual clarity — precise use of terms, clear definitions, no vagueness
Demonstrated understanding of argumentation — not just WHAT positions exist, but WHY something supports or refutes a claim
Genuine engagement over landscape surveys — taking the argument somewhere rather than listing views
what_the_examiner_values.desired_depth: The level of a sharp, enthusiastic undergraduate who grasps the main and most well-known arguments in analytic philosophy, with sparks of an opinionated approach
what_the_examiner_values.opinionated_approach: Some visible positioning is welcomed and rewarded — the essay should show a thinker who cares about the topic, not a neutral reporter

content_problems: Advanced academic opinions or obscure digressions that would be unusual for an undergraduate to encounter through normal study — this looks suspicious rather than impressive
Mere surveying of positions without engaging with the arguments behind them
Being too assertive without providing supporting argument
Not addressing the asked topic or question directly
style_problems: Dry, purely formal academic prose sustained for long stretches — formal arguments must be woven together with clear, accessible explanations
what_the_examiner_penalises.scope_rule: Non-standard or non-mainstream arguments should only appear when the question explicitly calls for them and specifies which ones to use

phrases_that_signal_quality: This can be objected to on the grounds that ...
The strongest version of this argument holds that ...
However, this faces the following difficulty ...
In support of this, we can note that ...
